query: AlCrFeNiSi belongs to a high-entropy-alloy family developed to combine properties that traditional single-principal-element alloys often cannot achieve simultaneously. Earlier research sought stable solid solutions and adjusted HEA compositions to target particular properties, but tradeoffs persisted: the CoCrFeMnNi system has limited wear and corrosion resistance, manganese can promote oxidation and oxide spallation, and cobalt-containing systems raise cost and processability concerns. Conventional bulk fabrication can cause compositional segregation during cooling, whereas mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing techniques can generate residual thermal stresses that impair mechanical performance and increase processing complexity. Given cobalt-free AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock, what single intervention could improve mechanical integrity while limiting segregation, residual stress, and defect formation? State one hypothesis containing the intervention, its causal mechanism, a quantitative or directional outcome relative to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the processing and test boundaries of validity, the prior evidence supporting it, and a decisive experiment that could falsify it.

falsification_experiment.design: compare the mechanical properties of AlCrFeNiSi fabricated using L-PBF with high scanning speeds to those fabricated using conventional methods
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: if the tensile strength and fracture strain of L-PBF fabricated AlCrFeNiSi are not significantly improved (by 5% or more) compared to conventionally fabricated AlCrFeNiSi, the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: Medium entropy alloy (MEA) is a hot spot in the field of material research in recent years. At present, the most widely used processing method of MEAs is “casting-rolling-heat treatment”, and the preparation of CoCrNi MEA by laser additive manufacturing (LAM) is still in primary stage. In this study, CoCrNi MEAs were fabricated with different scanning speeds by laser additive manufacturing, and the influence of scanning speed on its mechanical properties was investigated. The results show that higher scanning speed can significantly improve the mechanical properties of CoCrNi MEA. Compared with the low-speed laser additive manufacturing (LSLAM) MEA, the tensile strength of high-speed laser additive manufacturing (HSLAM) MEA is increased by 5.6 % and the fracture strain is increased by 60 %, which is mainly due to the entanglement of 1/6<112> and 1/2<110> dislocations and the defect structure at the grain boundary. LAM is a promising technology that can promote the development and application of MEAs in industry.

Multi-component alloys containing Co, Cr, Ni and other elements have attracted attention recently []. Equiatomic CoCrNi MEAs in particular demonstrate high strength and ductility at low temperatures []. CoCrNi MEAs are typically manufactured by casting and powder metallurgy, yielding a room temperature yield strength of only 360 MPa. Higher mechanical properties require additional processing like rolling, heat treatment and high pressure torsion []. Mechanical alloying (MA) combined with spark plasma sintering (SPS) can also produce CoCrNi MEAs with improved mechanics []. Traditional casting has some shortcomings such as low solidification rate, element segregation and rough casting microstructure, which requires heat treatment to optimize the structure. Compared to traditional casting, LAM can fabricate complex geometries []. LAM enables high cooling rates and temperature gradients, yielding refined solid solution phases and microstructures well-suited for high quality CoCrNi MEAs. Research on CoCrNi MEAs with LAM remains limited. There are many articles on LAM of CoCrNi MEAs. but there are very few articles on HSLAM CoCrNi MEAs. Additive manufacturing (AM) is rapidly emerging as a pivotal technology for industrial part production due to its ability to create intricate shapes through computer-assisted layer-by-layer part construction. In metal AM, a broad, ever-expanding technology landscape has emerged with varying degrees of adoption in industry. While various AM technologies exist, liquid-mediated metal AM, notably Laser Powder Bed Fusion (L-PBF), has garnered significant interest in industry and academia due to its potential to produce high-quality parts. L-PBF’s quality relies on understanding the interplay between process parameters, material properties, and solidification conditions. Traditional alloy design primarily targets specific manufacturing routes and often overlooks the unique demands of additive manufacturing (AM). In AM, designing alloys requires optimizing both chemistry and processing conditions simultaneously to minimize defects and enhance reliability. Conventional approaches first focus on achieving target properties and then on developing scalable processing methods.
